summary: Describes a way for an SSH client and server to agree on a shared secret using RSA public-key encryption instead of Diffie-Hellman. It needs much less computing time on the client, which helps slow devices. It is a proposed standard from 2006.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4432 gives SSH a second way to agree on a session key. The server sends a temporary RSA public key. The client makes up a random secret, locks it with that key and sends it back. Only the server can unlock it. Both sides then mix the secret with the details of the connection to produce a hash, which the server signs with its usual host key, so the client can be sure it is talking to the right server.

questions: faster ssh key exchange for slow clients
what is ssh rsa key exchange
what is the ssh exchange hash
subtitle: A faster SSH key exchange that lets a slow client lock a random secret to the server's temporary RSA key.

tldr.problem: The Diffie-Hellman key exchange in SSH can take tens of seconds on a slow CPU, which is irritating for the user of a small device.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a transient RSA public key, the client encrypts a random secret with it and sends it back, and both sides hash the secret with the session parameters into an exchange hash that the server signs with its host key.
tldr.outcome: The client does one RSA encryption instead of a Diffie-Hellman computation, which is an order of magnitude less client CPU time. RFC 4432 was later updated by RFC 9142.

today: RFC 4432 was published in March 2006 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9142. The two method names it registers are still the RSA key exchange methods an SSH client may be offered.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Secure Shell is a secure remote-login protocol. The core protocol uses Diffie-Hellman key exchange. On slow CPUs, this key exchange can take tens of seconds to complete, which can be irritating for the user.

A previous version of the SSH protocol, described in the SSH1 paper, uses a key-exchange method based on Rivest-Shamir-Adleman public-key encryption, which consumes an order of magnitude less CPU time on the client, and hence is particularly suitable for slow client systems such as mobile devices. This memo describes a key-exchange mechanism for the version of SSH described in RFC 4251 that is similar to that used by the older version, and about as fast, while retaining the security advantages of the newer protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual SSH handshake is heavy on the client because the client does the expensive part of the Diffie-Hellman computation. Doing the expensive part on the server instead makes a small device much faster.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The RSA key-exchange method consists of three messages. The server sends to the client an RSA public key, K_T, to which the server holds the private key. This may be a transient key generated solely for this SSH connection, or it may be reused for several connections. The client generates a string of random bytes, K, encrypts it using K_T, and sends the result back to the server, which decrypts it.

The client and server each hash K, K_T, and the various key-exchange parameters to generate the exchange hash, H, which is used to generate the encryption keys for the session, and the server signs H with its host key and sends the signature to the client. The client then verifies the host key as described in section 8 of RFC 4253.

This method provides explicit server identification as defined in section 7 of RFC 4253. It requires a signature-capable host key.
sections.plainLanguage: Three messages do the work: the server's public key, the client's locked secret, and the server's signature. Everything else follows from the usual SSH rules.

sections.title: Details
sections.content:
The method has the parameters HASH, the hash algorithm for calculating the exchange hash, HLEN, the output length of HASH in bits, and MINKLEN, the minimum transient RSA modulus length in bits. Their values are defined in sections 5 and 6 for the two methods defined by the document.

First, the server sends SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_PUBKEY, the server public host key and certificates K_S as a string, and K_T, the transient RSA public key, as a string. The key K_T is encoded according to the ssh-rsa scheme described in section 6.6 of RFC 4253. Unlike an ssh-rsa host key, K_T is used only for encryption and not for signature, and the modulus of K_T MUST be at least MINKLEN bits long.

The client generates a random integer K in the range 0 <= K < 2^(KLEN-2*HLEN-49), where KLEN is the length of the modulus of K_T in bits. The client then uses K_T to encrypt K as an mpint. The encryption is performed according to the RSAES-OAEP scheme of RFC 3447, with a mask generation function of MGF1-with-HASH, a hash of HASH, and an empty label. The client then sends SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_SECRET carrying the string RSAES-OAEP-ENCRYPT(K_T, K). The last stage of RSAES-OAEP-ENCRYPT is to encode an integer as an octet string using the I2OSP primitive of RFC 3447, which, combined with encoding the result as an SSH string, gives a result that is similar but not identical to the SSH mpint encoding of that integer. This is the same encoding used by ssh-rsa signatures in RFC 4253.

The server decrypts K. If a decryption error occurs, the server SHOULD send SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT with a reason code of SSH_DISCONNECT_KEY_EXCHANGE_FAILED and MUST disconnect. Otherwise, the server responds with SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_DONE carrying the signature of H with the host key.

The hash H is computed as the HASH hash of the concatenation of the client's identification string V_C, the server's identification string V_S, the payload of the client's SSH_MSG_KEXINIT, the payload of the server's SSH_MSG_KEXINIT, the host key K_S, the transient RSA key K_T, the encrypted secret RSAES_OAEP_ENCRYPT(K_T, K), and the shared secret K as an mpint. This value is called the exchange hash and is used to authenticate the key exchange. The exchange hash SHOULD be kept secret.

The signature algorithm MUST be applied over H, not the original data. Most signature algorithms include hashing and additional padding, so in a case such as ssh-dss, which specifies SHA-1 hashing, the data is first hashed with HASH to compute H, and H is then hashed again as part of the signing operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The server proves who it is by signing the hash of everything both sides know: the version strings, the negotiated algorithms, the host key, the temporary key, and the secret.

sections.title: The Two Methods and Their Message Numbers
sections.content:
The rsa1024-sha1 method specifies RSA key exchange with SHA-1 as the hash, an HLEN of 160, and a MINKLEN of 1024.

The rsa2048-sha256 method specifies RSA key exchange with SHA-256 as the hash, an HLEN of 256, and a MINKLEN of 2048.

Three message numbers are defined: SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_PUBKEY is 30, SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_SECRET is 31, and SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_DONE is 32.
sections.plainLanguage: Two named versions are offered, one with a 1024-bit key and SHA-1, and one with a 2048-bit key and SHA-256.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations in RFC 4251 apply.

If the RSA private key generated by the server is revealed, then the session key is revealed. The server should thus arrange to erase this from memory as soon as it is no longer required. If the same RSA key is used for multiple SSH connections, an attacker who can find the private key, either by factorising the public key or by other means, will gain access to all of the sessions that used that key. As a result, servers SHOULD use each RSA key for as few key exchanges as possible.

RFC 3447 recommends that RSA keys used with RSAES-OAEP not be used with other schemes, or with RSAES-OAEP using a different hash function. In particular, K_T should not be used as a host key, or as a server key in earlier versions of the SSH protocol.

Like all key-exchange mechanisms, this one depends for its security on the randomness of the secrets generated by the client, the random number K, and the server, the transient RSA private key. It is essential that the client use a high-quality cryptographic pseudo-random number generator to generate K. Using a bad random number generator will allow an attacker to break all the encryption and integrity protection of the Secure Shell transport layer.

The size of transient key used should be sufficient to protect the encryption and integrity keys generated by the key-exchange method. The strength of RSAES-OAEP is in part dependent on the hash function it uses. RFC 3447 suggests using a hash with an output length of twice the security level required, so SHA-1 is appropriate for applications requiring up to 80 bits of security, and SHA-256 for those requiring up to 128 bits.

Unlike the Diffie-Hellman key-exchange method defined by RFC 4253, this method allows the client to fully determine the shared secret K. This is believed not to be significant, since K is only ever used when hashed with data provided in part by the server, usually in the form of the exchange hash H. If an extension to SSH were to use K directly and to assume that it had been generated by Diffie-Hellman key exchange, this could produce a security weakness, so protocol extensions using K directly should be viewed with extreme suspicion.

This key-exchange method is designed to be resistant to collision attacks on the exchange hash, by ensuring that neither side is able to freely choose its input to the hash after seeing all of the other side's input. The server's last input is in SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_PUBKEY, before it has seen the client's choice of K, and the client's last input is K and its RSA encryption, and the one-way nature of RSA encryption should ensure that the client cannot choose K so as to cause a collision.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things carry the security: the server's private key must stay secret and must not be reused, and the client's random number must really be random. A predictable random number would break the whole session.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned the names rsa1024-sha1 and rsa2048-sha256 as Key Exchange Method Names in accordance with RFC 4250.
sections.plainLanguage: The two method names are registered so that clients and servers can agree on them during negotiation.

viz.caption: THE THREE MESSAGES OF THE RSA KEY EXCHANGE

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_PUBKEY (30)
messages.note: Carries the host key K_S and the transient RSA public key K_T.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_SECRET (31)
messages.note: Carries the random secret K encrypted with K_T.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_DONE (32)
messages.note: Carries the signature of the exchange hash H with the host key.
